prompt: What does a delivery stream do that a Kinesis data stream does not?
hint: One of them needs a consumer program.

choices.text: Keeps records in order per partition key
choices.why: That is the data stream's promise, per shard.

choices.text: Writes what it receives into S3, with no code of yours
choices.why: Right. It gathers records into buffers and writes each buffer as an object.

choices.text: Keeps records for up to 365 days, so that they can be replayed
choices.why: That is a data stream's longest retention; a delivery stream keeps nothing to replay.

choices.text: Lets several consumers read the same records at once, each at its own pace
choices.why: Several readers is what a data stream offers; a delivery stream has one destination.

prompt: An object written from `batch.json` reads `{...}{...}` on one line. Why can Athena not read it as two orders?
hint: What did Firehose put between the two records?

choices.text: moto corrupted the bytes; AWS would have written valid JSON
choices.why: This part moto does faithfully: by default Firehose concatenates records exactly so.

choices.text: Athena reads only Parquet
choices.why: Athena reads JSON lines; the problem is that there are not two lines.

choices.text: By default Firehose adds no delimiter, and the records carried no newline
choices.why: Right. The producer ends each record with `\n`, or a processor adds one.

choices.text: `put-record-batch` wraps records in a JSON array that Athena rejects
choices.why: No array was written; the bytes were simply joined.

prompt: At 13:10 in São Paulo, Firehose wrote an object under `raw/orders/2026/10/16/16/`. What is the `16` before the object name?
hint: São Paulo is three hours behind UTC.

choices.text: The hour in UTC
choices.why: Right. The default dated part is the UTC hour of arrival, 16 for 13 in São Paulo.

choices.text: The day of the month, repeated
choices.why: The day is the `16` before it; the last part is the hour.

choices.text: The number of the buffer written that day, counting from the first
choices.why: Firehose numbers no buffers in the key; the object name carries a time and a random suffix.

choices.text: The size of the object in megabytes
choices.why: The key carries the date only; the size is the object's metadata.

prompt: In the lab, three calls to a delivery stream with hints of 64 MB and 300 seconds produced three objects within a second. How many would AWS have written?

choices.text: Three, one per call, since each call is a request
choices.why: That is moto's behaviour; AWS buffers across calls.

choices.text: Four, one per record
choices.why: Firehose never writes an object per record unless each record fills a buffer alone.

choices.text: One, after the interval ended, holding all four records
choices.why: Right. A few hundred bytes are far from 64 MB, so the 300 seconds write the buffer.

choices.text: None until 64 MB arrived
choices.why: The interval writes a buffer that has not filled; that is what it is for.

prompt: A quiet delivery stream never fills its 64 MB buffer, and its interval is 600 seconds. How many objects does it write in a day?
hint: A day is 86,400 seconds, and the interval writes every buffer.

prompt: moto accepted a delivery stream with `SizeInMBs` 500 and `IntervalInSeconds` 5000 and answered `ACTIVE`. What follows?

choices.text: Those values work on AWS, which also accepts them
choices.why: A success from moto means the request was well formed; these are outside AWS's ranges.

choices.text: AWS refuses them: they are outside its documented ranges
choices.why: Right: the size goes up to 128 MB and the interval up to 900 seconds. The refusal was not run here.

choices.text: moto rounded them down to the maximum and kept the stream
choices.why: `describe-delivery-stream` printed 500 and 5000 back, unchanged.

prompt: A quiet stream writes 288 objects of 3.5 MB a day into the lake, and the readers can wait fifteen minutes for data. What is the first change?

choices.text: Raise the size to 128 MB
choices.why: The size is never reached now; a larger size changes nothing while the interval writes every buffer.

choices.text: Raise the interval to 900 seconds, for 96 objects of about 10.4 MB
choices.why: Right. The interval is what writes them, and fifteen minutes is the delay the readers accept.

choices.text: Turn on dynamic partitioning, which merges small buffers
choices.why: It splits the stream into more buffers, each smaller.

choices.text: Turn on GZIP
choices.why: Compression makes the same number of objects smaller still.

prompt: On AWS, a delivery stream's `Prefix` is `raw/orders-dt/dt=!{timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd}/`. What comes between that prefix and the object's name?
hint: The documented rule depends on whether the prefix uses a timestamp expression.

choices.text: Nothing: Firehose adds no dated part after a timestamp expression
choices.why: Right. moto added `2026/10/16/16/` anyway, which is moto's and not AWS's.

choices.text: The UTC hour, `2026/10/16/16/`, which Firehose adds after every prefix
choices.why: That is what moto did; AWS adds it only when the prefix has no timestamp expression.

choices.text: The literal text `!{timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd}`, kept as it was written
choices.why: On AWS the expression is evaluated, into `2026-10-16`; text is what moto left.

choices.text: The partition key of the record
choices.why: A delivery stream fed directly has no partition key; values from records need dynamic partitioning.

prompt: With dynamic partitioning on and a prefix of `store=!{partitionKeyFromQuery:store}/`, where does a record with no `store` field go on AWS?
hint: It cannot be put in a folder named after a value it lacks.

choices.text: Under `store=null/`
choices.why: Firehose makes no folder for a missing value.

choices.text: It is dropped silently
choices.why: The error prefix exists so that a failure is not a silence.

choices.text: Under the error output prefix
choices.why: Right, with `!{firehose:error-output-type}` naming why.

choices.text: Under `store=pinheiros/`, the first store seen
choices.why: Each record is partitioned by its own value, never another record's.

prompt: Why is the customer id a bad key for dynamic partitioning of Quitanda's orders, although it is a good partition key for the Kinesis stream?
hint: Each distinct value gets a buffer of its own.

choices.text: jq cannot read a field with a hyphen in its value
choices.why: jq reads any string value.

choices.text: Customer ids are personal data and may not appear in a key
choices.why: An opaque id like `c-17` is what the lake already keys records by; the problem here is count.

choices.text: Tens of thousands of buffers, each written nearly empty by the interval: tiny objects
choices.why: Right. A shard needs many keys to spread; a folder layout needs few values to stay large.

choices.text: Kinesis and Firehose hash the key differently, so customers end up in the wrong folder
choices.why: Dynamic partitioning does not hash; it uses the value itself.

prompt: An object written by a stream with `CompressionFormat` `GZIP` in moto starts with the bytes `{"order_id"`. What does that show?

choices.text: That moto stored the bytes uncompressed
choices.why: Right. moto keeps the configuration and compresses nothing.

choices.text: That GZIP compresses only objects over 5 MB
choices.why: There is no such threshold; on AWS every object would be compressed.

choices.text: That `aws s3 cp` decompressed the object on the way down
choices.why: `aws s3 cp` copies bytes as they are stored.

prompt: Which of these does AWS need for record format conversion to Parquet? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where does the schema come from, and what may the input be?

choices.text: A table in the Glue Data Catalog that gives the columns
choices.why: Right; the stream reads the schema from it.

choices.text: Records in JSON
choices.why: Right; JSON is the input conversion accepts.

choices.text: `CompressionFormat` set to `GZIP`
choices.why: It stays `UNCOMPRESSED`; Parquet compresses inside, here with `SNAPPY`.

choices.text: A Lambda function that writes the Parquet
choices.why: Conversion is Firehose's own; no function is involved.

choices.text: A buffer of at least 64 MB
choices.why: Right; AWS sets that minimum when conversion is on.

prompt: A transformation Lambda also adds each order's total to a running sum in a database. What can go wrong?
hint: What does Firehose do with a batch whose call timed out?

choices.text: Firehose refuses functions that write to a database
choices.why: Firehose cannot see what a function does inside.

choices.text: Nothing: each record reaches the function once
choices.why: A failed or timed-out batch is retried, so a record can reach the function twice.

choices.text: A retried batch adds the same orders to the sum again
choices.why: Right. The side effect is performed once per attempt; lesson 23 is about making it safe.

choices.text: Records marked `Dropped` are added twice
choices.why: `Dropped` only keeps a record out of S3; it says nothing about what the function did.

prompt: In the lab, a record put into the Kinesis stream `orders` never reached the delivery stream that names it as its source. What is true on AWS?
hint: moto keeps the source in the configuration and reads nothing.

choices.text: The same: Firehose reads a Kinesis source only when asked with a call
choices.why: On AWS it reads the stream continuously, as a consumer.

choices.text: Firehose reads it continuously, and refuses any `PutRecord` sent straight to it
choices.why: Right. moto got both halves the other way round, so the pairing was configured and not observed.

choices.text: Records reach S3 only after the stream's retention period ends
choices.why: Firehose reads as records arrive, then buffers them.

prompt: A producer sends 2 million records a day of 1 KB each to Firehose for 30 days. Each record is billed rounded up to 5 KB, at 0.05800 USD per GB ingested. What is the month's ingestion, in USD? Take 1 GB as 1,000,000 KB.
hint: 2 million × 5 KB a day, then 30 days.

prompt: Why did packing five events into one record cut the Firehose ingestion from 174.00 to 34.80 a month?
hint: What is the smallest size a record is billed at?

choices.text: The 5 KB billed minimum is now full, where four fifths of it was wasted
choices.why: Right. The bytes sent did not change; the rounding stopped wasting four fifths of each record.

choices.text: Firehose compresses larger records
choices.why: Nothing was compressed; the billed size fell because of the rounding.

choices.text: Fewer records mean fewer objects in S3, and objects are what Firehose bills
choices.why: Objects come from buffers, not records, and the S3 bill is separate.

choices.text: Batches of five go into the cheaper price tier
choices.why: The first tier runs to 500 TB; both cases are in it.

prompt: Records Firehose cannot deliver as configured are written under the ___, which may name the failure with `!{firehose:error-output-type}`.
hint: It is a key of the destination configuration, next to `Prefix`.

prompt: Put in order what happens on AWS to an order event sent to a delivery stream that converts to Parquet and partitions by store.
hint: The store has to be read before the record can join a buffer.
items: The producer sends the record, ending in a newline
The record waits in that store's buffer
The buffer reaches 128 MB or 900 seconds
The buffer is converted to Parquet with the Glue table's schema

prompt: Quitanda's only use for a new event stream is a copy in S3, readable within fifteen minutes. What fits best?
hint: Which half of lesson 20's pairing would have no reader?

choices.text: A Kinesis data stream with 7 days of retention, read by a program that writes S3
choices.why: That rebuilds Firehose by hand and pays for retention nobody reads.

choices.text: A delivery stream fed directly, with a 900-second interval
choices.why: Right. With no other consumer, the data stream in front would add cost and no reader.

choices.text: A Kinesis data stream in front of a delivery stream, for ordering
choices.why: Nothing here needs per-key order, and objects interleave shards anyway.

choices.text: A delivery stream with a 60-second interval, so the data arrives soonest
choices.why: Fifteen minutes was allowed; sixty seconds makes fifteen times the objects for nothing.
